q1: Render the page in standards mode. The doctype declaration switches the browser from legacy quirks mode into modern HTML5 standards mode, ensuring consistent cross-browser rendering.
q2: No — it is not an HTML element. `<!DOCTYPE html>` is a processing instruction, not a tag, so it never has a closing counterpart.
q3: <head> holds machine-readable metadata. It contains the title, meta tags, and links to external resources — none of which are rendered as visible content.
q4: One <body> element is the rule. It is the single container for all visible, interactive content on the page.
q5: html → head → body is the correct order. The <html> root wraps everything; <head> comes first, then <body>.
q6: The browser switches to quirks mode when the doctype is missing. Quirks mode emulates old browser behaviour, causing inconsistent rendering especially around the box model.
q7: Sets the browser tab text and search-result title. The <title> is metadata — it appears in the browser tab and as the clickable link in search engine results, but not on the page itself.
q8: Visible and interactive content lives in <body>. Everything the user sees and interacts with — text, images, forms, buttons — belongs here.
q9: Browsers silently move it to <body> or ignore it. HTML parsers are very forgiving and attempt error recovery, but you should never rely on this behaviour.
q10: It causes inconsistent rendering and box-model behaviour. In quirks mode the box model and many CSS properties work differently across browsers, making layouts unpredictable.
